questions.question: Which statement best describes the expectation of a random variable in the context of model evaluation?
questions.choice_A: It is the long-run average value the variable would take if the data-generating process were repeated indefinitely.
questions.choice_B: It is the most probable value observed in any single finite dataset.
questions.choice_C: It is the value that minimizes the maximum possible error over all outcomes.
questions.choice_D: It is the median of the empirical distribution of the observed sample.

questions.question: When reporting variability of a performance metric across runs, why is standard deviation often preferred over variance?
questions.choice_A: Variance is undefined for heavy-tailed distributions.
questions.choice_B: Standard deviation has the same units as the original metric, making it easier to interpret.
questions.choice_C: Variance is biased while standard deviation is always unbiased.
questions.choice_D: Standard deviation is invariant to linear transformations while variance is not.

questions.question: What does a Z-score of $z = -2$ for a model’s per-example loss indicate after standardization?
questions.choice_A: The loss is two units less than the raw mean in original units.
questions.choice_B: The loss is two median absolute deviations below the median.
questions.choice_C: The loss is two standard deviations below the mean of the loss distribution.
questions.choice_D: The loss is twice as likely as the mean loss to occur.

questions.question: Which of the following is a primary purpose of mean subtraction followed by division by standard deviation when normalizing features?
questions.choice_A: To reduce the sample size requirements for hypothesis testing.
questions.choice_B: To make features uniformly distributed on $[0,1]$ for all components.
questions.choice_C: To guarantee independence between features and labels.
questions.choice_D: To put features on comparable scales, which can stabilize and speed up optimization.

questions.question: An estimator $\hat{\theta}_n$ is called unbiased for parameter $\theta$ if:
questions.choice_A: $\mathbb{E}[\hat{\theta}_n] = \theta$ for the data-generating distribution.
questions.choice_B: $\hat{\theta}_n \to \theta$ almost surely as $n \to \infty$.
questions.choice_C: $\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\theta}_n)$ is minimized among all estimators.
questions.choice_D: $\hat{\theta}_n$ achieves the Cramér–Rao lower bound.

questions.question: Which statement about the sample mean $\bar{X}$ as an estimator of the population mean $\mu$ is correct under i.i.d. sampling?
questions.choice_A: It is unbiased only for normal distributions.
questions.choice_B: It is consistent as sample size increases.
questions.choice_C: It has zero variance when $n>30$.
questions.choice_D: It is always more efficient than the sample median for any distribution.

questions.question: In null-hypothesis significance testing (NHST), a $p$-value is best interpreted as:
questions.choice_A: The probability that the null hypothesis is true given the data.
questions.choice_B: The probability of observing data as extreme or more extreme than what was observed, assuming the null is true.
questions.choice_C: The Type II error rate of the test procedure.
questions.choice_D: The minimum effect size detectable with power 0.8.

questions.question: A 95% confidence interval (CI) for a mean, constructed from i.i.d. data under standard assumptions, can be interpreted as:
questions.choice_A: There is a 95% probability that the true mean lies in this specific computed interval.
questions.choice_B: In repeated sampling and interval construction, 95% of such intervals would contain the true mean.
questions.choice_C: The interval contains 95% of future observations with probability 1.
questions.choice_D: It guarantees that the $p$-value of the associated test is below 0.05.

questions.question: Which scenario exemplifies the bias–variance tradeoff in model training?
questions.choice_A: A highly flexible model fits noise in training data, leading to low training error but high test error.
questions.choice_B: A rigid model achieves low training and low test error simultaneously.
questions.choice_C: A flexible model achieves higher bias and lower variance.
questions.choice_D: A rigid model achieves lower bias and higher variance.

questions.question: What is the main idea behind Monte Carlo estimation of an expectation $\mathbb{E}[f(X)]$?
questions.choice_A: Deriving a closed-form integral for $f$ using symbolic methods.
questions.choice_B: Approximating the expectation by averaging $f(X_i)$ over random samples $X_i$ drawn from the distribution of $X$.
questions.choice_C: Minimizing $f$ via gradient descent over the support of $X$.
questions.choice_D: Approximating $f$ with a polynomial and integrating the polynomial exactly.

questions.question: If features are standardized to zero mean and unit variance, which property holds for any single feature dimension across the dataset?
questions.choice_A: Its empirical covariance with every other feature is zero.
questions.choice_B: Its empirical distribution is approximately normal.
questions.choice_C: Its empirical mean is 0 and empirical variance is 1 by construction.
questions.choice_D: Its correlation with the target is unchanged compared to unstandardized features.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes a sampling distribution?
questions.choice_A: The distribution of the population parameter across individuals.
questions.choice_B: The distribution of observed covariates in the dataset.
questions.choice_C: The joint distribution of features and labels under the model.
questions.choice_D: The distribution of a statistic (like the mean) computed from repeated samples of the same size from the population.

questions.question: Why is correlation insufficient to establish causation in evaluating interventions on model performance?
questions.choice_A: Because correlation only measures nonlinear dependence, not linear dependence.
questions.choice_B: Because confounders and reverse causality can create associations that are not due to a direct causal effect.
questions.choice_C: Because correlation cannot be computed without randomized experiments.
questions.choice_D: Because causation requires the correlation to be exactly 1.

questions.question: Which estimator property is most directly about the distribution of the estimator shrinking around the true parameter as sample size grows?
questions.choice_A: Unbiasedness
questions.choice_B: Consistency
questions.choice_C: Sufficiency
questions.choice_D: Robustness

questions.question: In the context of standardization, what happens to the covariance matrix of features after applying per-feature mean subtraction and scaling by each feature’s standard deviation?
questions.choice_A: It becomes the identity matrix, regardless of original correlations.
questions.choice_B: Its diagonal entries become 1, while off-diagonal entries equal the pairwise correlations.
questions.choice_C: All entries become 0 due to decorrelation.
questions.choice_D: It becomes singular for any dataset with more features than samples.

questions.question: Suppose you use Monte Carlo with $n$ i.i.d. samples to estimate an expectation with finite variance. How does the estimator’s standard error typically scale with $n$?
questions.choice_A: It is constant in $n$.
questions.choice_B: It scales as $1/n$.
questions.choice_C: It scales as $1/\sqrt{n}$.
questions.choice_D: It scales as $1/n^{3/2}$.

questions.question: Which situation illustrates high bias and low variance in model predictions?
questions.choice_A: Predictions are consistently off-target in the same direction across datasets.
questions.choice_B: Predictions vary widely across datasets but average out to the true value.
questions.choice_C: Predictions match the training data perfectly but generalize poorly.
questions.choice_D: Predictions are unbiased with small mean squared error.

questions.question: You compute a 95% CI for the mean validation accuracy using a normal approximation, but the sample size is small and the distribution is skewed. What is the most appropriate concern?
questions.choice_A: The CI may undercover or be misleading because the normal approximation may be poor.
questions.choice_B: The CI is guaranteed to be conservative in small samples.
questions.choice_C: The CI is invalid unless the data are exactly normal.
questions.choice_D: The CI remains exact due to the central limit theorem.

questions.question: What is a practical risk when normalizing inputs using statistics computed on the test set?
questions.choice_A: It reduces the variance of estimators, improving generalization.
questions.choice_B: It introduces label leakage without affecting input distributions.
questions.choice_C: It leads to data leakage, inflating reported performance and invalidating evaluation.
questions.choice_D: It prevents overfitting by removing test-time distributional shifts.

questions.question: Which statement correctly links variance, standard deviation, and mean squared error (MSE) for an unbiased estimator $\hat{\theta}$?
questions.choice_A: MSE$(\hat{\theta}) = \mathrm{Var}(\hat{\theta}) + \theta^2$
questions.choice_B: MSE$(\hat{\theta}) = [\mathbb{E}(\hat{\theta}) - \theta]^2$
questions.choice_C: MSE$(\hat{\theta}) = \mathrm{Var}(\hat{\theta})$
questions.choice_D: MSE$(\hat{\theta}) = \sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\theta})}$
